items.x: The share of predictions that match the label. Misleading when one class is rare: always predicting the majority class can score well.
The area under the ROC curve: the chance that a randomly chosen 1 gets a higher score than a randomly chosen 0. 0.5 is a random ranking and 1 a perfect one; no threshold is involved.
Grow many deep trees, each on a bootstrap sample of the training rows, and average their forecasts. The average cancels much of what one tree gets wrong by chance.
The simplest rule a model has to beat: the training average, the majority class, or persistence. A score means little until it sits next to the baseline's.
Bias is the error of a model too simple to follow the truth; variance the error of a model so flexible it follows the noise of its training rows. More flexibility trades the first for the second.
Start from the mean and add small trees one at a time, each fitted to what the trees so far still get wrong and shrunk by the learning rate.
As many rows as the data, drawn at random with replacement, so some rows come twice and about a third not at all.
Whether a probability means what it says: of the days given 0.3, about 30 percent should turn out to be 1s.
Predicting a label, such as whether next month will be busier than this one, rather than a number.
The four counts behind every score of a classifier: true positives, false positives, false negatives and true negatives.
Choosing between models with the training rows only: fit on some folds, score on the next, and average. Time-series folds always score rows that come after the ones fitted on.
Information the forecast could not have had at the time, slipping into a feature or into the fit, such as a scaler fitted on the test rows. It makes a model look better than it is.
A model that asks one question of one column at a time and forecasts the mean, or the class shares, of the training rows in each leaf.
Add trees until the score on later rows stops improving, and keep the number of trees at which it was best.
The ridge and lasso penalties at once, in a mix set by l1_ratio.
The harmonic mean of precision and recall, which sits close to the smaller of the two.
A column used to predict, built only from what was known when the forecast is made.
How much a model leans on each column: from its cuts, measured on the training rows, or by permutation, on rows it did not fit.
One of the blocks the training rows are cut into for cross-validation.
How mixed the labels in a box are: 2p(1 - p) for two classes, and zero when the box is pure. A classification tree cuts where it falls most.
The direction in which a loss rises fastest. For squared error, minus the gradient is the residual, which is why boosting fits its trees to residuals.
Trying every value of a setting on the folds and keeping the best; GridSearchCV then refits it on all the training rows.
A setting chosen before fitting, such as alpha, C, k, the depth of a tree or the number of trees. Chosen on validation rows, never on the test rows.
Classify a row by a vote among the k training rows closest to it, on standardised columns.
Linear regression with a charge on the sum of the absolute coefficients. It sets some coefficients to exactly zero.
The share of each new tree that boosting adds. A smaller rate needs more trees for the same fit.
What logistic regression minimises: minus the log of the probability given to what happened. A confident wrong probability costs the most.
A linear model for a label: a weighted sum of the columns, put through the sigmoid to become a probability.
The mean absolute, mean squared and root mean squared error of a forecast of a number. The RMSE is in the target's own units.
Predicting the most common label everywhere: the baseline for accuracy.
A value far from normal tends to be followed by one closer to normal, such as a calm month after a busy one.
Forcing a model's forecast to rise, or to fall, as one column rises, everything else unchanged.
Scoring each training row with the trees whose bootstrap sample left it out. Fair for separate cases; too kind on days, whose neighbours were in the sample.
Learning the noise of the training rows along with their pattern: a lower training error and a higher test error.
A charge on the size of the coefficients, added to what the fit minimises, with a strength set by alpha, or by 1/C in logistic regression. Also called regularisation.
How far a model's score falls when one column is shuffled, on rows the model did not fit.
Forecasting that the next value equals the latest one: next month's volatility is this month's. Hard to beat in finance.
Steps chained into one model, such as a scaler and then ridge, so cross-validation refits every step inside every fold.
Of the times the model said yes, the share that were right.
Bagging in which each question chooses among a few columns drawn at random, so the trees differ more and their average is steadier.
Of the real yeses, the share the model caught.
How a tree grows: the best single cut, then the best cut inside each new box, never revising an earlier one.
Predicting a number, such as next month's volatility.
What happened minus what was forecast.
The relative change in a price, (p1 - p0) / p0. The log return, log(p1 / p0), adds up over time.
Linear regression with a charge on the sum of the squared coefficients: every coefficient shrinks towards zero, none to exactly zero.
The recall against the false positive rate, at every threshold.
1 / (1 + exp(-z)): turns any number into a probability between 0 and 1.
The sigmoid for more than two classes: exponentiate each class's score and divide by the total.
Subtract a column's mean and divide by its standard deviation, both learned on the training rows.
A tree with one question and two leaves.
Learning a rule from rows whose answer is known. Unsupervised learning looks for structure with no answer column.
The column to predict, set on the row of the features it is predicted from.
Rows held back until the end and used once, to score the model that was chosen.
The probability from which a classifier says 1. The default is 0.5; when the two mistakes cost different amounts, another threshold is cheaper.
The rows a model is fitted on.
Scoring candidates on rows they were not fitted on, before the test rows: the folds, or a later block.
The standard deviation of returns: how much a price moves. Annualised by the square root of 252 trading days.

Every argument of an object and its current value. help(Ridge) prints the documentation.
A label from a comparison: True and False become 1 and 0. Its mean is the share of ones, and predicting the majority class everywhere is the accuracy a model has to beat.
The classifier, shown with its defaults: a ridge penalty of strength 1/C, solved in at most 100 steps. Create it, then .fit(X, y), as for every model.
The fitted numbers, on the log-odds scale. coef_ has one row per boundary between classes, so coef_[0, 0] is the first slope.
With one column: the value of the column at which the probability is one half, where .predict() switches from 1 to 0.
The odds factor: one unit more of a column multiplies the odds of a 1 by this. A coefficient adds to the log-odds; its exponential multiplies the odds.
The classes, in the order predict_proba uses for its columns.
One row per observation, one column per class, each row summing to one. [:, 1] is the probability of a 1.
The 0/1 predictions: 1 where the probability of a 1 is at least one half.
Predictions at any other threshold, from the probability column. The model is unchanged; only the comparison changed.
How many steps the solver took. Log-loss has no formula for the coefficients, so .fit() improves them step by step; raise max_iter when the ConvergenceWarning appears, or standardise first.
The objective, averaged over the rows: minus the log of the probability given to what happened. A confident wrong probability costs the most.
The share of predictions that match the label. True labels first, predictions second, like every metric. Compare it with the majority rule.
A 2 by 2 array: rows are what happened, columns are the prediction, both in the order of classes_. Top left true negatives, bottom right true positives.
The share of predicted 1s that were 1. Falls when the threshold falls.
The share of real 1s that were predicted. Falls when the threshold rises.
Returns fpr, tpr, thresholds: the false positive rate and the recall at every threshold where a point moves. Joined up, the ROC curve.
The area under the ROC curve: 0.5 for a random ranking, 1 for a perfect one, no threshold involved. Pass the probabilities, never the 0/1 predictions.
One score per fold; larger is better, so no minus sign. Other strings: "accuracy", "neg_log_loss", "precision", "recall".
The strength of the penalty, upside down: C = 1/alpha, so a small C is a strong penalty. Standardise in a pipeline first and choose C on a grid in factors of ten.
A grid for GridSearchCV: the step name, two underscores, the argument. Then GridSearchCV(pipe, grid, cv=folds, scoring="roc_auc").fit(X, y), and best_params_, best_score_, predict_proba as before.

The lasso's penalty on a classifier, which sets coefficients to exactly zero. It needs a solver that can handle absolute values; the default lbfgs cannot. scikit-learn 1.8 and later retire penalty: there it is LogisticRegression(l1_ratio=1, solver="liblinear", C=0.01).
The 2 by 2 array flattened into tn, fp, fn, tp, in reading order. The four counts every other score is built from.
Count each class in inverse proportion to its size while fitting. Raises recall on a rare class and lowers accuracy, leaves the AUC alone, and breaks the probabilities.
The whole precision-recall curve in one number. Its no-information line is the share of ones, not 0.5, so report the two together. More informative than AUC when the class is rare.
Returns precision, recall and the thresholds, for drawing the curve or reading the precision at a recall you care about.
The mean squared error of the probabilities, with what happened as 1 or 0. Smaller is better. It separates two models that the AUC cannot tell apart.
Wrap a model and learn a second, small model mapping its numbers onto probabilities, on folds. It repairs a distorted level; it cannot repair a base rate that has changed since fitting.
Precision, recall and F1 for every class, with the macro and weighted averages underneath. labels= sets the order.
One F1 per class, averaged equally. "weighted" averages by class size instead, and None returns the scores themselves. Read macro when the class you care about is the small one.
The matrix with the rows and columns in an order you choose rather than alphabetically. Without it the middle row of a three-class matrix is rarely the class you expect.
The raw score per class, before the exponential and the division that turn scores into probabilities.
The softmax: make every score positive, then divide by the total so they add to one. With two classes it is the sigmoid.

items.t: move[p >= t].sum() - move[p <= 1 - t].sum() - cost * n_trades
items.x: A bet on the direction, in money: long where the probability of a rise is at least t, short where it is at most 1 - t, every trade paying a cost. The best t rises with the cost; choose it on the training rows.
Classify a row by a vote among the k training rows closest to it. Works for any number of classes with no change.
The scaler is not optional here: distance is dominated by whichever column has the largest spread, so an unscaled model reads only that one.
A small k fits the training rows and little else; k of 1 scores a perfect training AUC. A large k is a simple model, the way a small C was.
A grid for GridSearchCV. k cannot exceed the SMALLEST fold, not the training size; above that the search returns nan and warns.
The share of the k neighbours in each class, so the probabilities are multiples of 1/k. A small k gives coarse ones.
k-NN can take a category as one plain number: once the columns are scaled, the nearest rows to a Monday at 18:00 are Mondays near 18:00. A logistic regression needs the weekday as columns instead.

A tree for a number. Each question compares one column with a cut, and each leaf forecasts the mean of its training rows. max_depth caps the questions on any path; without it the tree splits until it fits the training rows almost exactly.
Another way to keep a tree small: no leaf may hold fewer training rows than this. Choose it, or max_depth, on the folds.
Grow the tree, then prune it: a question stays only if it lowers the training error by at least ccp_alpha for each leaf it adds. The default, 0, keeps every question.

A tree for a label. The same cuts, chosen by Gini, 2p(1 - p) for two classes, which is twice the squared error of the 0s and 1s per row. Each leaf holds the share of each class, which predict_proba returns.

items.t: plot_tree(tree, feature_names=columns, filled=True, impurity=False, precision=3, fontsize=9)
items.x: Draw a fitted tree with matplotlib: every box shows its question, the rows that reached it and its forecast. filled shades the boxes by their forecast, impurity=False drops the error line, and label="root" names the fields in the top box only.
For a classification tree: name the classes in the order of classes_, and show each box's shares instead of its counts.
The questions on the longest path, and the number of leaves. A tree grown without a limit ends with about one leaf per training row.
Inside a fitted tree: the column number and the cut of the first question, so columns[tree.tree_.feature[0]] is its name. The boxes are numbered depth first, and a leaf has feature -2.
The number of the leaf each row lands in. Group any column by it to see what each leaf holds.
Bagging: grow a deep tree on each of 25 bootstrap samples of the training rows and average their forecasts, which cancels much of what one tree gets wrong by chance.
The fitted trees inside a bagging model or a forest, as a list, each a tree like any other. They were fitted on plain arrays, so give their predict X.to_numpy().

A forest: bagging in which each question chooses among a few columns drawn at random, here the square root of their number, so the trees differ. The default for a number, max_features=1.0, is plain bagging; RandomForestClassifier's default is already "sqrt".

Out-of-bag: each training row is forecast by the trees whose sample left it out, so the forest scores itself without folds. Fair on rows that are separate cases; too kind on days, whose neighbours were in the sample.
The forest for a label. forest.oob_decision_function_[:, 1] is each training row's out-of-bag probability of a 1.
Grow the trees on every core at once. GridSearchCV takes n_jobs too, and then fits the folds side by side instead.
A grid for a model on its own, outside a pipeline: the argument name with no step name in front. GridSearchCV(DecisionTreeRegressor(random_state=0), grid, cv=folds, ...) as before.

items.t: RandomizedSearchCV(model, grid, n_iter=10, cv=folds, scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error", random_state=0)
items.x: Try n_iter combinations drawn at random from the grid instead of every one; best_params_ and best_score_ as for GridSearchCV. For grids too big to run in full.
The fits a search will make: one per combination on each of five folds, and one refit on all the training rows. Time one fit and multiply before you press run.
Read a clock, in seconds. time.perf_counter() - start after a fit is how long it took.

Boosting: start from the mean of y, then add n_estimators small trees one at a time, each fitted to the residuals of the forecast so far and shrunk by learning_rate. max_depth=1 makes every tree a stump; the default is 3. A smaller learning_rate needs more trees for the same fit.
The same for a label. The trees are added on the log-odds scale, each fitted to y minus the probability so far, and predict_proba turns the sum into probabilities.
The forecast after 1, 2, 3, ... trees, up to n_estimators. staged_predict hands them out one at a time, so list() collects them: [49] is the forecast after 50 trees.

Early stopping inside scikit-learn: hold back a random tenth of the training rows and stop once 10 more trees have not helped on them. boost.n_estimators_ is the number of trees it grew. A random tenth suits separate cases and is too kind on days.

scikit-learn's fast boosting: each column is first sorted into at most 255 bins, and cuts fall only between bins. max_iter is the number of trees. Above 10,000 rows it stops early on its own, on a random tenth of them, unless early_stopping=False. It has no feature_importances_.

XGBoost, with the methods every scikit-learn model has: fit, predict, and predict_proba on XGBClassifier. It cuts each column only between 256 bins and puts a light ridge penalty on the leaf values. Its own defaults are learning_rate=0.3 and max_depth=6, so set both.
Early stopping in XGBoost: score every new tree on the rows given to fit as eval_set, and stop 50 trees after the best score. n_estimators is then only a ceiling.
The rows that stop it, as a list of (columns, target) pairs: rows later than those fitted on, never the test rows. verbose=False keeps it from printing the score of every tree.
Where the score on eval_set was best, counting the first tree as 0, and that score. predict then uses the first best_iteration + 1 trees.
The number of trees early stopping found, refitted on all the training rows, the block that chose it included. The refit takes no eval_set and no early_stopping_rounds.

XGBoost's record of the score after every tree, for each eval_set entry, under validation_0, validation_1, ... in the order given. Plot it against the number of trees to see the curve early stopping read.
The score early stopping watches. The default is the log loss for a label and the RMSE for a number; "auc" stops at the best AUC instead.

reg_lambda is the ridge penalty on the leaf values. subsample and colsample_bytree give each tree a random share of the rows and of the columns, as a forest does. Settings to try after the depth and the number of trees, not before.
XGBClassifier: the sum of the trees before the sigmoid, on the log-odds scale. 1 / (1 + np.exp(-margin)) gives back predict_proba(X)[:, 1].
Never let the forecast fall as a column rises, everything else unchanged: 1 for a column that may only raise the forecast, -1 for one that may only lower it, by its name in the table given to fit.

LightGBM. It grows each tree leaf by leaf, splitting whichever leaf lowers the error most, so num_leaves sets the size of a tree: 2 makes a stump, and the default is 31. verbose=-1 silences its messages.

items.t: boost.fit(X, y, eval_set=[(X_stop, y_stop)], eval_metric="auc", callbacks=[early_stopping(50, verbose=False)])
items.x: Early stopping in LightGBM: a callback passed to fit rather than a setting of the model. boost.best_iteration_ counts the first tree as 1, where XGBoost's best_iteration counts it as 0.
LightGBM's best score, by data set and metric. For a number the metric is the squared error, l2, so its square root is the RMSE.

How much the model used each column, one number per column in column order. scikit-learn's trees sum each column's fall in the error and scale the total to one, XGBoost averages the fall per cut, and LightGBM counts the cuts. Measured on the training rows, so a column of noise can still collect many cuts.
Make LightGBM sum the fall in the loss on each column instead of counting its cuts. XGBoost takes importance_type too, where "weight" counts the cuts.

items.t: permutation_importance(boost, X_test, y_test, scoring="roc_auc", n_repeats=10, random_state=0)
items.x: For any model: shuffle one column at a time on rows the model did not fit, and record how far the score falls, n_repeats times for each column. A column of noise falls by about zero.
Per column, in column order: the mean fall in the score over the repeats, and its spread. pd.Series(result.importances_mean, index=columns) names them.
A name Python has never seen. Usually a typo, or a cell you have not run yet.
The right operation on the wrong kind of thing. Often text where a number belongs, or a placeholder ... left in a cell.
A position that does not exist. A list of 5 stops at index 4.
A dictionary key, or a column name, that is not there.
Python could not read the line at all. Look for a missing bracket, quote or colon.
Dividing by zero. Often an empty list you thought had something in it.
The package is not installed, or you are running a different Python.
The path is wrong relative to where you are running from.
Two arrays whose dimensions do not fit. Check .shape on both.
A matrix with no inverse: one column carries nothing the others do not. Perfect multicollinearity.
The columns given to predict are not the ones fit saw, in the same order. Select them with the same list both times.
Must have at least 1 validation dataset: XGBoost was given early_stopping_rounds but no eval_set to score the trees on. Pass eval_set to fit, or leave early_stopping_rounds out of a refit.
Not an error: the solver ran out of steps before the coefficients settled. Raise max_iter, or standardise the columns first.

A number, a list of numbers, a table of numbers. That is the whole inventory. Everything in this course is built from three objects, and most confusion about a formula is really confusion about which of the three a symbol refers to. Object Written here Example Shape In NumPy Scalar a single number lower case italic: x, λ, n x = 3.5 no shape 3.5 Vector a list of numbers bold lower case: x, β x = …

items.l: Maths brush-up · Three kinds of object
items.x: R is the set of all real numbers, meaning every ordinary number. Built from it: x ∈ Rx is a single real number x ∈ R^px is a list of p real numbers X ∈ R^n × pX is a table of real numbers with n rows and p columns y_i ∈ 0, 1the target takes one of the two values in that set λ ≥ 0λ is a number that is never negative The symbol ∈ is read is in, or belongs to. A line like X ∈ R^n× p looks forbidding …

If the shapes fit, the expression means something. If they do not, it is not a hard formula, it is a mistake. The single most useful habit in this course: write the shape under every symbol. A matrix expression is only legal when the shapes line up, so checking shapes catches most errors before you have understood anything else, and it tells you what an unfamiliar expression is going to produce. …

Subscripts say which row, which column, or which of something else. Most of the time there are only two of them. Two indices do nearly all the work, and they always mean the same thing: i = 1, …, nruns down the rows, over observations j = 1, …, pruns across the columns, over features Which gives three things that look alike and are not: Written Is a Means x_ij scalar the value of feature j for …

items.l: Maths brush-up · Indices, subscripts and sums
items.x: Read: the sum, over i from 1 to n, of a_i. The Σ is a capital Greek sigma, and it is shorthand for a loop that adds things up. In Python it is sum(...), or a for loop with total += a. Everything you need to know about it: The letter under the Σ is the counter. It exists only inside the sum, exactly like the loop variable in for i in range(n). Limits are often dropped once they are obvious, so Σ_i …

items.l: Maths brush-up · Indices, subscripts and sums
items.t: Hats, bars and the difference between them
items.x: xx bar: the sample mean of x βbeta hat: an estimate of β, computed from data. The hat is the whole difference between the truth and your guess at it. y_ithe model's prediction for observation i, as against y_i, what actually happened fyour fitted model, as against f, the true relationship nobody ever sees The hat is not decoration. β is a fixed unknown number; β is a number you calculated, which …

A list of numbers with an agreed order. The one operation that matters is the dot product, and it is a weighted sum. By convention a vector is a column unless it is transposed. So x ∈ R^3 is 3 × 1, and x^ᵀ, read x transpose, is the same numbers laid out as a row, 1 × 3. Same three numbers. Only the shape changed, and shape is what decides whether the next multiplication is legal. Adding two …

Multiply the two lists entry by entry, then add up. The result is a single number: (1 × p)(p × 1) = 1 × 1. You already use this constantly, under other names. A portfolio with weights w = (0.5, 0.3, 0.2) holding assets that returned r = (0.02, -0.01, 0.04) earned A portfolio return is a dot product. So is a fitted value: replace the weights with coefficients and the returns with features, and y_i …

items.t: Length, and the two norms you need
items.x: x _2the Euclidean norm, Σ_j x_j^2. Ordinary straight-line length. For (3,4) it is 9+16=5. x _2^2the same thing squared, so just Σ_j x_j^2 = x^ᵀx, a sum of squares. This is the form you actually meet, because it drops the square root. x _1the _1 norm, Σ_j |x_j|. Add up the sizes, ignoring signs. For (3,-4) it is 7. Double bars are a norm, of a vector. Single bars are either absolute value, of a …
A table of numbers, and a few special ones with names. A ∈ R^m × n has m rows and n columns, and a_ij is the entry in row i, column j. Rows first, always. A matrix is square if m = n.

The transpose A^ᵀ flips the table over its diagonal: rows become columns. An m × n matrix becomes n × m, and a_ij moves to position ji. In NumPy: A.T. Two rules to keep: (A^ᵀ)^ᵀ = A, and (AB)^ᵀ = B^ᵀA^ᵀ, which reverses the order. That second rule is used in the OLS derivation below. Two notations, one meaning. Econometrics usually writes the transpose as a prime, X', and says X prime. Machine …

I or I_pthe identity: ones down the diagonal, zeros everywhere else, p × p. It is the matrix version of the number 1, in that AI = IA = A. In NumPy, np.eye(p). diagonalzero off the diagonal. Multiplying by one just rescales each entry. symmetricA^ᵀ = A, so it is unchanged by a flip. X^ᵀX is always symmetric, and so is a covariance matrix. 0a vector or matrix of zeros. In bold it is not the number …

Every entry of the answer is one dot product. Nothing more is going on. To multiply A (m × n) by B (n × k), the inner dimensions must match. Then entry (i, j) of the product is row i of A dotted with column j of B: Row from the left, column from the right. Say it once out loud and the formula stops being a formula. Worked out, with A being 2 × 3 and B being 3 × 2, so the product is 2 × 2: Top …

items.t: Two ways to read X β
items.x: Both readings are useful, and switching between them is most of what "thinking in matrices" means. Row by row Each entry of X β is one observation's features dotted with the coefficients: (X β)_i = x_i^ᵀ β. So X β is all n predictions at once. This is the reading to use when you want to know what the model does. Column by column X β = β_1 X_1 + … + β_p X_p, a weighted sum of the feature columns. …

items.t: Vectorisation: from n equations to one
items.x: The one idea that makes matrix notation worth learning. If you take one thing from this page, take this section. Write the linear model for a single observation i, the way it is usually introduced: This is n separate equations, one per trading day, all with the same unknown coefficients. Two compressions turn that into a single line. First, the right-hand side of each equation is a dot product, …

Where OLS comes from, and the one thing that stops it from existing. For a square matrix A, the inverse A^-1 is the matrix that undoes it: It is the matrix version of dividing by a number. There is no "matrix division", so this is how you move a matrix from one side of an equation to the other. A^-1 is not a power, and not 1/A. The superscript -1 is a name for an operation, not an exponent, and …

items.l: Maths brush-up · Inverses, singular matrices, and multicollinearity
items.x: Look at the recipe: it divides by the determinant. If (A) = 0 there is nothing to divide by and the inverse does not exist. Such a matrix is called singular. The three ways of saying it are worth collecting, because different sources use different ones: singularno inverse exists (A) = 0the determinant is zero rank deficientthe columns are not linearly independent: one of them is a weighted sum of …

items.l: Maths brush-up · Inverses, singular matrices, and multicollinearity
items.x: Now put that into a regression. OLS needs (X^ᵀX)^-1, and X^ᵀX is singular exactly when a column of X is a weighted sum of the others. That is perfect multicollinearity, and when it happens there is no unique answer: infinitely many β give exactly the same fitted values, so the data cannot choose between them. Reading it through the column-by-column view above, if one column duplicates a mix of …

items.t: Solving a matrix equation, and where OLS comes from
items.x: You are not asked to reproduce this derivation in this course. You are asked to read it without flinching. Start with the scalar case, which you know. To solve ax = b for x, divide both sides by a, which works as long as a ≠ 0. The matrix version replaces division by multiplication by the inverse, and because order matters you must multiply both sides on the same side: The middle step used A^-1A …

items.l: Maths brush-up · Solving a matrix equation, and where OLS comes from
items.x: Differentiating with respect to a vector means taking the derivative with respect to each entry and collecting the results into a vector. Two results cover the derivation below, and both are the obvious generalisation of the scalar case: Compare (d)/(dx)(ax) = a and (d)/(dx)(ax^2) = 2ax. Same statements, one dimension up. The symmetry condition holds here because X^ᵀX always is symmetric.

items.l: Maths brush-up · Solving a matrix equation, and where OLS comes from
items.x: OLS chooses the β that makes the residual sum of squares as small as possible. Write that objective, expand it, differentiate, set to zero. 1 The objective, in matrix form: 2 Multiply it out, using (AB)^ᵀ = B^ᵀA^ᵀ: The two cross terms are each single numbers, and a number equals its own transpose, which is why they combine into one term with a 2. 3 Differentiate with respect to β and set the …

Every model in this course is defined as the solution to a minimisation, so you need to know what "the minimum" means operationally. (df)/(dx), f'(x)the derivative: the slope of f at x. Positive means going up as x increases, negative means going down. ( f)/( β_j)a partial derivative: the slope in the β_j direction with every other coefficient held fixed. The curly is what signals "there are …

items.l: Maths brush-up · Derivatives, gradients and minima
items.x: OLS and ridge have closed-form solutions: a formula you can evaluate directly. Lasso, logistic regression, and everything built out of trees do not. For those, the answer is found by walking downhill, and the notation for one step is: Read: the next guess is the current guess, moved a little way in the direction the loss falls fastest. η (eta) is the learning rate, the size of the step. The …

items.t: Sums, logs, exponentials and the sigmoid
items.x: Where the strange-looking classification formulas come from. Three rules of logarithms carry all the weight, and only the first really matters: In this field log means the natural logarithm, base e ≈ 2.718, which some texts write . It is np.log in NumPy. The first rule is why likelihoods are always logged. The probability of seeing n independent observations is a product of n terms, which is …

Mostly one symbol you already know, plus the convention about capital letters. X, Ycapital letters are random variables: the thing before you observe it x, ylower case is a realisation: the value it actually took. So P(Y = 1 | X = x) asks about a particular observed x. P(A)the probability of A, a number between 0 and 1 P(A | B)the vertical bar is read given: the probability of A once B is known. …

Needed for k-nearest neighbours, and for understanding why standardising is not optional there. The distance between two observations is the length of the vector between them: The Euclidean distance: Pythagoras in p dimensions. Subtract feature by feature, square, add, take the root. The _1 version, Σ_j |x_j - z_j|, is the Manhattan distance, and both show up as options in scikit-learn. Now …

Half the models in this course are defined by one template, and once you can read the template each new model is a one-line change. First, the notation for a minimisation: Read: the β that makes L as small as possible. The subscript names what you are free to vary. min L is the smallest value of L; min L is the argument that achieves it. In a model definition you almost always want the second, …
The arithmetic behind how a model is judged and chosen: the scores of a classifier, the cross-validation estimate, the bootstrap, and the softmax.

items.l: Maths brush-up · Scores, folds and samples
items.x: Every score of a classifier is built from the four counts of the confusion matrix: TP and TN, the right answers, FP, the false alarms, and FN, the misses. Precision asks how often a yes was right; recall, how many of the real yeses were caught. F_1 is their harmonic mean, which stays close to the smaller of the two. Accuracy, (TP + TN)/n, is the mean of an indicator, as in the section on trees …

items.l: Maths brush-up · Scores, folds and samples
items.x: Cut the training rows into K folds, score the model on each fold after fitting it on the others, and average. With time-series folds the model is only ever fitted on rows that come before the fold it is scored on. The setting with the smallest CV_(K) wins, and only then are the test rows used, once.

items.l: Maths brush-up · Scores, folds and samples
items.x: A bootstrap sample draws n rows from n, with replacement. Each draw misses a given row with probability 1 - 1/n, so about 37 percent of the rows are left out of each sample and 63 percent are in. A forest can forecast each row with only the trees whose sample left it out: the out-of-bag forecast. On days it flatters the forest, because a day left out has its neighbours in the bag.

items.l: Maths brush-up · Scores, folds and samples
items.x: With N classes the model gives each class a score s_j. The exponential makes every score positive, and the division makes the N probabilities add up to one. With two classes it is the sigmoid, applied to the difference between the two scores.
Tree formulas look unlike regression formulas, but they use only two new pieces of notation.

items.l: Maths brush-up · Notation for trees and ensembles
items.x: Also written I(A) or 1_A. It turns a yes-or-no question into a number so it can be used in arithmetic. In Python it is exactly what (s > 0).astype(int) does, from the Session 4 cheatsheet: a comparison produces True and False, and the cast makes them 1 and 0. With it, "count how many of these are true" is Σ_i 1…, and "what fraction are true" is (1)/(n)Σ_i 1…. Accuracy is a mean of indicators, …

items.l: Maths brush-up · Notation for trees and ensembles
items.x: A regression tree cuts the feature space into M non-overlapping boxes R_1, …, R_M, the leaves, and predicts one constant in each. Written out, the whole model is: Every term is zero except the one box the observation falls into, so the sum picks out a single c_m. It is a lookup table written as a sum, which is a pattern worth recognising: a sum over regions with an indicator is nearly always …

items.l: Maths brush-up · Notation for trees and ensembles
items.x: Once there are many trees, an extra index appears for which tree, usually b or m. There are only two ways to combine them, and the notation tells you which one you are looking at: Average them (bagging, random forest) B trees are grown independently on different resamples, then averaged. The 1/B is the giveaway: independent votes, equal weight. Averaging cuts variance, which is why a forest beats …

The formulas you will actually be shown, each read out symbol by symbol. This is the drill: cover the notes, read the equation aloud, then check. None of these is derived here, and several belong to later sessions. The point is only that by now you should be able to say what every symbol in them is, and what shape it has. If you can do that, an unfamiliar model is a short read rather than a wall. …

The same objects, in the language you will write them in. Everything here is on the cheatsheet except where noted. Symbols that mean different things depending on where they sit. These are the ones that cause real confusion in an exam. Machine Learning in Finance · Session 1 Programming and machine learning for people who have never written a line of code. We start from zero.

The academic part Jonas Theill Bøjstrup, PhD student Research: image-based prediction in finance and deep learning Teaching this course for the second time Supervised 6+ master’s theses The rest of me Art collector Video games Becoming a dad in December Questions any time, in class or by email to jobo@econ.au.dk, whoever is lecturing. Bezirgen Veliyev lectures some of the sessions.

Everyone uses itThe dominant language in data science and quantitative finance. What you learn transfers to a real job. Batteries includedFree libraries for data, statistics, and machine learning: pandas, scikit-learn, and many more. ReadablePython code reads close to plain English. That matters enormously when you are starting out. Endless helpA vast community. Almost any error you hit has been asked and answered somewhere already. Free, open, and runs anywhere: later in the course, also on your own laptop with no internet.

Finance has become a data discipline. Asset management, risk, trading, credit, fintech: all increasingly run on models fit to data. Job postings that used to ask for “econometrics” now ask for machine learning. You already know one such model: ordinary least squares. This course extends that instinct to more flexible tools. The goal is not to make you a computer scientist. It is to let you read, build, and judge the models that finance now runs on.
Your OLS regression is already a simple machine-learning model: it learns its coefficients from data. We build outward from there.

1 to 3Python: variables, loops, functions and dictionaries; NumPy, pandas and matplotlibfrom today 4foundations of machine learning: features, targets, splits and scoresno model yet 5 and 6model selection and cross-validation; ridge and lassothe first models 7a house in Aarhus, with every tool so fara case lecture 8 and 9classification: logistic regression, thresholds and k-NNlabels 10tomorrow’s power price in West Denmarka case lecture 11 and 12trees, forests and boosted treesflexible models 13the two cases with trees, and the examthe wrap-up Thirteen sessions, from the week of 31 August 2026 (week 36) to week 42.

In class Lectures We work through concepts together, with live code you can see running. This is where ideas are introduced. At home Exercises A notebook of short practice tasks each week, with hints and solutions folded in. This is where the learning sticks. At home The case One financial investigation that grows through the course, a part after most sessions. You carry it forward each week. Lectures are for watching and understanding. You learn to code by doing the exercises and the case yourself, between sessions.

Zerono code, no ML ———▶7 weeks Python + MLfoundations you can build on Going from no programming to machine learning in seven weeks is a steep climb. Be ready for it. I can explain ideas and show code, but watching is not learning to code. You become fluent by doing it yourself. The exercises and case are where that happens. My job is to teach the concepts and point the way. Your job is to do the work.

AI assistants are useful and are not banned. Use them to learn, not to avoid learning. Helpful Explain an error message you do not understand Explain a concept a different way Suggest what a line of code does Generate extra practice problems Harmful Pasting in solutions you cannot reproduce Submitting code you do not understand Leaning on it instead of building skill Relying on it for the exam: you cannot A good test: if you could not rewrite it from memory afterwards, you have not learned it yet.

3 hours on site, at a fixed time No internet no AI, no web search, no Colab Your laptop Python running locally The exam runs on your own machine, offline. We begin in Google Colab because it is the easiest place to start, and later move to a local setup: a VS Code tutorial comes in Session 3. Because the exam is offline, the skill has to be yours. That is the whole reason the exercises matter.

By the end of this session you can: run Python in a notebook and say what the runtime remembers store values in variables and use the basic types of data hold many prices in a list and pick out any day or window compute a simple return from two prices read a Python error message calmly And you meet the course case: a four-part risk report on real US stocks.
Part 1 Where our code lives, and how a code cell shows its result.

items.t: A notebook is a stack of cells
items.x: text Compute this week’s return [ ] (248.83 - 183.56) / 183.56 0.3556 A notebook is a document read top to bottom, made of two kinds of cell. The result of a code cell appears directly beneath it.

Text cells hold explanation: headings, sentences, the story. Code cells hold Python, and can be run. Their output appears below. That is the whole idea. A lecture, a calculation, and its result can live in one scrollable document, which is exactly what these slides are. We begin in Google Colab, which runs notebooks in your browser with nothing to install. You need only a Google account.

Click into a code cell and press Ctrl + Enter. The cell runs and shows the value of its last line, and only the last one. These slides run Python too. Run this: just one number appears. A real Python cell, running in your browser. Change the numbers and run it again. Clicking Run does exactly the same thing.

items.t: The keys that run a cell
items.x: key what it does where Ctrl + Enter runs the cell, stays put everywhere, including these slides Shift + Enter runs the cell, moves to the next Colab, Jupyter, VS Code On a Mac, use Cmd in place of Ctrl. Shift + Enter is the habit most people settle into in Colab. The little editor built into these slides is the one place it does nothing at all, so here use Ctrl + Enter or the Run button.

items.t: Showing more than the last line
items.x: To show several values, use print(...): print is our first function: a named tool you use by writing its name and round brackets. It displays whatever you put inside, each on its own line. We will lean on it constantly.
Part 2 Expressions, and leaving notes to yourself.
An expression is code that produces a value. The text after a # is a comment: Python ignores it; it is a note for humans. Change the numbers and run it. Arithmetic works as you would expect.
items.c: comment shares each

items.x: write meaning + - * / add, subtract, multiply, divide ** power: 1.05 ** 10 is ten years of 5% growth ( ) grouping, exactly as in mathematics Order of operations is the usual one: powers, then * and /, then + and -. Parentheses override it.
1,000 invested at 4% for five years is a single expression: Change the rate to 0.06 and run again. Compounding is just repeated multiplication, written with **.
Part 3 Giving a value a name, so you can use it again.
A variable gives a value a name. The = sign means assign: “store this under that name”, not “equals”.
items.c: price shares

items.t: Once named, it stands for the value
items.x: Anywhere you write the name, Python uses the value: holding_value now holds the result, ready to reuse, with no need to retype the multiplication.
items.c: price shares holding_value

items.x: Assigning to a name that already exists replaces its value. The old one is gone. Read price = price * 1.02 from the right: take the current price, multiply by 1.02, and store the result back into price.
Line 2 uses price on both sides at once. What do you think that does, and what is price at the end? Reason it out before you run. Can a name really appear on both sides of =?
items.c: price

items.x: Python requires: letters, digits, and underscores only a name may not start with a digit no spaces: share price fails, share_price works case matters: Price and price are two different names
Both are legal. Only one will make sense to you next month: x = 0.0212 weekly_return = 0.0212 Write names for the person who reads the code later. That person is usually you, a week from now.
You bought 120 shares at 45.50 and sold at 48.10. Complete the cell to compute the profit. The result should be a little over 300.
items.c: shares buy_price sell_price profit

items.x: Part 4 Now that you can make variables: the notebook remembers them between cells.
Run this cell. It stores a value in memory under the name portfolio_value: The value is now held in memory. This memory is called the runtime.
items.c: portfolio_value

items.x: A later cell can use what an earlier cell defined, without repeating it: This works only because the cell above ran first and left portfolio_value in memory. A notebook is not just text on a page. It has a memory that fills up as you run cells.
items.c: portfolio_value

items.x: Cells can be run in any order you click them, and the runtime only knows what it has been told so far. Run a page top to bottom and all is well. Jump around, and a cell may look for something that does not exist yet. The next two cells show it.

items.x: Fresh runtime: nothing has defined bonus yet. What do you think happens when you run this? Talk it through before you press Run. Does Python guess a value? Refuse? Something else?

items.x: Give bonus a value, and the very same expression works: The error before was not a fault in the code: the runtime simply had nothing stored under that name. Define it first, and all is well.
items.c: bonus

items.x: When a notebook gets confusing, reset it: Runtime → Restart and run all. A notebook is only trustworthy if it runs cleanly top to bottom from a fresh start. We will hold to that all course. Restarting clears the runtime’s memory and re-runs every cell in order. It fixes almost every “but it worked a minute ago” mystery.
Part 5 Numbers, text, and true/false, and why the difference costs money.
Python tells you the type of any value with the type(...) function: int for whole numbers: share counts, trading days float for numbers with a decimal point: prices, returns, rates
items.c: type

items.x: Even when it divides evenly: The result is 25.0, a float, not 25. Division in Python always produces a decimal number.
A string is text inside quotes, such as tickers, names and dates:
items.c: ticker AAPL type

items.x: + between strings joins them. It does not add: "150" in quotes is text that looks like a number. It is not a number, and that difference causes real bugs, because prices read from files often arrive as text.

items.x: Both values are wrapped in quotes. What will + do here, and is it what you would want? Decide before you run. Talk to your neighbour first.
float(...) turns text into a number. Now it really adds: No error is not the same as no mistake. "10" + "5" gave "105" with no complaint, and a silently wrong answer is the dangerous kind.
items.c: float

A function takes input in parentheses and returns a value. Two new ones: round rounds to a number of decimals; len counts characters.

Apple’s closing price, first week of 2024, in a single list: A list collects values, in order, under one name.

Yesterday’s close p_0, today’s close p_1. The simple return is the percentage change in price: what one unit invested earned in a day. It is the basic object of this whole course. Deliberately familiar: the same percentage change you know from econometrics growth rates.

Now, together Opening Google Colab, saving your own copy, and running your first cells, live.
Machine Learning in Finance · Session 2
Last session you stored prices in a list, indexed it, and computed a simple return from two prices. That return is a single line: That is the return for one day, from the first close to the second.
items.c: prices

items.x: To study a stock you want every day’s return. Apple traded about 252 days in 2024, so that is 251 returns. Writing them out one line at a time, (prices[1] - prices[0]) / prices[0], then (prices[2] - prices[1]) / prices[1], and so on, is not realistic. You need a way to say: do this once for every day. That is a loop, and it is where we start today.

By the end of this session you can: repeat work automatically with a for loop and a while loop make choices with if package a calculation into a function you write yourself organise results by name in a dictionary combine all of it to measure risk properly, as volatility And you continue the course case: turning last session’s rough risk gauge into a real one.
Part 1 Doing something once for every item in a list.

Step through it one click at a time. Watch the highlighted line, and how the variable and the output change: prices = [183.56, 182.19, 179.87] for price in prices: print(price) variables price = 183.56 output take the first item variables price = 183.56 output 183.56 run the body variables price = 182.19 output 183.56 take the next item variables price = 182.19 output 183.56 182.19 run the body variables price = 179.87 output 183.56 182.19 take the next item variables price = 179.87 output 183.56 182.19 179.87 run the body variables no items left output 183.56 182.19 179.87 the list is finished, so the loop stops
Now run it for real. Instead of printing prices one by one, let Python walk the list: for price in prices: reads as “for each price in the list”. The indented line runs once per item.
items.c: prices price

items.x: Each time round, price holds the next value in the list: price is an ordinary variable, and you choose its name.
items.c: prices price close

items.x: Python knows what is inside the loop from the indentation: for price in prices: print(price) # indented: inside the loop, runs each time print("done") # not indented: runs once, after the loop The colon : opens the loop; the indented lines below it are its body.
Before running, decide how many lines this prints, and what they are. One line for each item, or something else? Press Run to check.
items.c: prices

items.t: Adding up a list, by hand
items.x: A loop can build a running total. Start at zero, then add each price: This is exactly what sum(prices) does. Now you can see inside it.
items.c: prices total price

items.x: That shape comes up constantly: start a variable at a neutral value (0 for a sum) update it once per item, inside the loop read it after the loop Set up, then loop and update, then use the result. Summing, counting, and averaging all follow this one pattern.

Updating a variable from itself, total = total + r, is so common that Python gives it a shorthand: total += r means total = total + r. The same works for -=, *=, and /=. We will use it for accumulators from here on.
items.c: total same

items.t: Looping a fixed number of times
items.x: range(n) gives the whole numbers 0, 1, ... , n - 1 to loop over: Use it when you care about positions, not the values themselves.
range(start, stop) begins at start and stops before stop: Just like slicing, the stop value is not included.
To compare each day with the one before it, loop over positions and use i and i - 1: Starting at 1 means the first pair is day 2 against day 1. There is no day before day 1.
items.c: prices after

items.x: To collect results, begin with an empty list and grow it with .append: [] is a list with nothing in it yet. This is how you gather values as a loop runs.
items.c: returns empty ready fill append

items.x: Put the two ideas together: loop over positions, and append each return: Five prices give four daily returns. The same formula as last session, now applied to the whole list.
items.c: prices returns append

items.x: Use a loop to add up all the returns into total. Start total at zero, and add each return inside the loop.
items.c: returns total

items.x: The accumulator pattern, on the returns: returns = [0.012, -0.004, 0.008, -0.011, 0.006] total = 0 for r in returns: total += r total Result: 0.011. Start at zero, add each return once, read the total after the loop.
Part 2 Running code only when a condition is true.
Last session a comparison gave True or False. if acts on that answer: The indented block runs only when the condition is True. Change price to 240 and run it again.

items.x: else handles what happens when the condition is False:
items.c: price above below

items.x: What does this print? Decide before you run it. Which branch is true when r is exactly zero?

items.x: Put the two together: check a condition for every item. Count the up-days: The if sits inside the loop body, indented once more. up_days grows only on positive days.
items.c: returns up_days

items.x: Each : opens a block, indented one step further than the last: for r in returns: # loop body: indented once if r > 0: # if body: indented twice up_days += 1 Read the indentation to see what belongs to what.
Count how many returns were negative (a down day).
items.c: returns down_days

items.x: The up-day count, with the comparison flipped: returns = [0.012, -0.004, 0.008, -0.011, 0.006] down_days = 0 for r in returns: if r < 0: down_days += 1 down_days Result: 2. Two of the five returns are below zero.
Part 3 Repeating for as long as a condition stays true.

items.t: When you do not know how many times
items.x: A for loop runs once per item. A while loop runs for as long as a condition holds, however many times that takes. How many years to grow 100 into 150 at 10% a year? You did not have to know the answer in advance. The loop keeps going until value reaches 150.
items.c: value years

items.x: Step through it. The condition is checked before each pass; watch value and years change: value = 100 years = 0 while value < 150: value *= 1.10 years += 1 variables value = 100.00 years = 0 100 < 150 ? yes, enter the loop variables value = 110.00 years = 1 grow value, count a year variables value = 121.00 years = 2 still below 150, go again variables value = 133.10 years = 3 still below 150, go again variables value = 146.41 years = 4 still below 150, go again variables value = 161.05 years = 5 grow value, count a year variables value = 161.05 years = 5 161.05 < 150 ? no, the loop stops

items.t: Careful: it must be able to stop
items.x: Something inside the loop has to move the condition towards False, or it runs forever: value = 100 while value < 150: years += 1 # value never changes, so this never stops A while loop needs an exit. Make sure each pass changes something the condition depends on. If a cell seems stuck, interrupt it with the stop button.
How many years to grow 1000 into 1500 at 8% a year? Complete the while loop. Two lines in the body: grow value, then count the year.
items.c: value years

items.x: value = 1000 years = 0 while value < 1500: value *= 1.08 years += 1 years Result: 6. After five years the value is still under 1500; the sixth year pushes it above.
Part 4 Naming a calculation once, so you can reuse it anywhere.
print, len, max, and sum are functions: a name, then inputs in brackets. Today you write your own.
def creates a function. You give it a name, its inputs, and what it returns:
items.c: simple_return

items.x: def simple_return(p0, p1): # name, and inputs (the parameters) return (p1 - p0) / p0 # the value it hands back def name(parameters): opens the function the indented body is what it does return hands a value back to whoever called it

items.t: Call it as often as you like
items.x: Once defined, a function can be used again and again: Write the formula once, and trust it everywhere. There is no copy to get wrong.

Part 6 Everything from today, combined into a real measure of risk.

Last session’s risk gauge used only two days, the highest and the lowest. A better measure uses every day’s return. That measure is volatility: how much the daily returns typically spread around their average.

Volatility is the standard deviation of the daily returns: In words: take each return’s distance from the average, square it, average those squares, and take the square root. It is the typical size of a daily move.

Each step is something you can already do: the daily returns, with a loop (Part 1) their average, sum(returns) / len(returns) each return’s squared distance from the average, averaged, then square-rooted with ** 0.5 We now build these into one function, one step at a time.

items.t: Build it up: the daily returns
items.x: Start the function with just step 1, the returns loop. It is not finished yet: def volatility(prices): returns = [] for i in range(1, len(prices)): returns.append((prices[i] - prices[i - 1]) / prices[i - 1]) # still to come: the average, and the spread So far it only collects the daily returns into a list.

Add step 2, the average return. Still not finished: def volatility(prices): returns = [] for i in range(1, len(prices)): returns.append((prices[i] - prices[i - 1]) / prices[i - 1]) mean = sum(returns) / len(returns) # still to come: the spread around the mean Now it also has the average of those returns.
Add step 3, the spread, and return it. Now it is complete, so run it: Every idea from today is here: two loops, an empty list, +=, and a return.

items.t: That is what a package is
items.x: A package is code somebody else wrote, that you can use by name. Three of them do most of the work in data analysis: NumPy numbers, vectors and matrices, and the maths on them pandas tables with named columns, like a spreadsheet you can program matplotlib figures, so you can see what you found There are thousands of others, and you will meet more of them as the course goes on, including scikit-learn, the one that fits models.

items.t: And they live on your machine
items.x: Packages are not part of Python. Somebody has to install them, and in Colab somebody already did. At the exam you sit with your own laptop, VS Code, and no internet. So today starts there: your machine, your packages, and how to look things up when you cannot search for them.

By the end of this session you can: work in VS Code on your own machine, and find documentation offline use NumPy for arrays, and for the matrix algebra behind every model use pandas to load, filter and summarise a real table of prices use matplotlib to turn a result into a figure somebody else can read And the case reaches all eleven stocks at once.
Part 1 VS Code, packages, and finding things out without the internet.

Colab still works, and the homework stays there. But: The exam three hours, your laptop, VS Code, offline. It should not be the first time. The editor helps you it completes names and shows documentation as you type It is yours your files, your packages, nothing to upload, no session that expires No internet needed once it is installed, it works on a train
The commonest confusion is thinking VS Code is Python. It is not: The setup guide installs all three.

VS Code opens .ipynb files: the same cells, the same Run buttons, the same output underneath as in Colab. Nothing about how you write code changes. Only where it runs. The exam is written in a notebook too. The first time you open one, VS Code asks which Python to use. Pick the one you installed, and it remembers.

Packages come from a public archive called PyPI. You install one once, and then it is on your machine for good: %pip install pandas Run that in a notebook cell, like any other code. The % marks it as an instruction to the notebook rather than to Python. Your setup guide already installed the three we need, so you should not have to type it at all today. Installing and importing are different. You install a package once, ever. You import it in every notebook that uses it.
import brings a package in. as gives it a short name: np, pd and plt are conventions, not rules. Everybody uses them and every tutorial assumes them, so use them too.

Part 2 Arrays: doing arithmetic to a whole list at once.

items.t: From lists of numbers to tables of them
items.x: So far, one row of numbers. NumPy’s other subject is the matrix: rows and columns of them. You have done all of this maths in econometrics. Nothing on the next few slides is a new idea. What is new is that each one takes a single line.

Vector A row or column of numbers. One stock’s returns, or a set of portfolio weights. Matrix A rectangle of numbers, n rows by p columns. One row per observation. Transpose Flip rows and columns. An n × p becomes a p × n. Dot product Multiply pairwise, then add up. Weights times returns is a portfolio return. Matrix product Only fits if the first one’s columns match the second one’s rows. Inverse The matrix that undoes another one. Exists only if no column is redundant.

items.t: A matrix is a list of rows
items.x: Three rows, two columns. shape always tells you which is which.
items.c: array shape

items.x: [row, column], and : means “all of them”. The same slicing as a list, once per direction.
items.c: one element first row second column

items.x: .T flips it: A 3 by 2 becomes a 2 by 3. You use this constantly, because it is how you make two shapes fit together.
items.c: shape

items.x: Multiply pairwise and add up. In finance that is a portfolio return: weights times returns. 0.5 × 0.012 + 0.3 × (-0.004) + 0.2 × 0.008. The @ symbol is matrix multiplication, and for two vectors that is the dot product.
items.c: weights array returns

items.x: Three rows in, three numbers out: one per row. That is a regression’s fitted values, for the whole sample in one go.
items.c: array

items.x: Nearly every NumPy error you will ever see is this rule.

np.linalg.inv gives the matrix that undoes another one: The result is the identity: ones down the diagonal, zeros elsewhere. The off-diagonal one prints as something like -1.11e-16, which is scientific notation for a decimal point followed by fifteen zeros and a 111. Computers store decimals approximately, so a value that should be exactly zero often comes out this tiny instead. Read it as zero.
items.c: array linalg inv

items.x: B = np.array([[1.0, 2.0], [2.0, 4.0]]) np.linalg.inv(B) LinAlgError: Singular matrix The second column is just twice the first, so it adds nothing. You have met this before under another name: perfect multicollinearity, the regression that will not run.

Your econometrics course wrote the estimator like this: beta = np.linalg.solve(X.T @ X, X.T @ y) Read it against the formula: X.T is X', @ is multiplication, and solve does the inverting and multiplying in one safer step.

Apple’s daily return against the market’s. The slope is the beta you know from the CAPM: Change the ticker and run it again: Nvidia gives 1.75, JPMorgan 1.12, Coca-Cola 0.60. Above one moves more than the market, below one moves less.

items.x: Squaring a million numbers, first with a loop and then with an array: import time xs, arr = list(range(1_000_000)), np.arange(1_000_000) t0 = time.perf_counter() total = 0 for v in xs: total += v * v loop = time.perf_counter() - t0 t0 = time.perf_counter() total = (arr * arr).sum() vec = time.perf_counter() - t0 print(f"loop: {loop:.3f} s numpy: {vec:.4f} s {loop / vec:.0f} times faster") loop: 0.084 s numpy: 0.0026 s 32 times faster NumPy hands the whole array to compiled code, instead of stepping through it one Python statement at a time.

items.t: What to check before you show it
items.x: Does it have a title? Say what the reader is looking at. Are the axes labelled? With units. “price (USD)”, not “price”. Can you tell the lines apart? A legend, or a name written on the line. Do the bars start at zero? Lines need not. Bars must. Is anything decorative? If it carries no information, remove it. Would a stranger get it? Without you standing there to explain.

items.t: It can look much better than this
And here is what that cost
items.x: fig = plt.figure(figsize=(11, 4)) gs = fig.add_gridspec(2, 1, height_ratios=[3, 1], hspace=0.12) ax, ax2 = fig.add_subplot(gs[0]), fig.add_subplot(gs[1], sharex=ax) for a in (ax, ax2): for side in ("top", "right"): a.spines[side].set_visible(False) ax.plot(s.index, s.values, color="#1c5cab", linewidth=1.5, zorder=3) for i, alpha in enumerate(np.linspace(0.16, 0.01, 14)): ax.fill_between(s.index, s.values * (i / 14), s.values * ((i + 1) / 14), color="#1c5cab", alpha=alpha, linewidth=0, zorder=1) ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(mtick.StrMethodFormatter("${x:,.0f}")) ax.axvspan(peak, trough, color="#b8860b", alpha=0.10, zorder=0) ax.annotate("peak", xy=(peak, s.loc[peak]), xytext=(-52, 22), …

items.t: So learn the four calls first
items.x: Get the plot right, then make it pretty, and only if it is worth the time. When you do want it prettier, go to the matplotlib gallery at matplotlib.org. It is a wall of example charts, each with the code that made it. Find the picture closest to what you want, and read how it was done. That is how everybody learns plotting, including the people who do it for a living.

Now that you have a machine with folders on it: fig.savefig("figures/nvda_2024.png", dpi=200, bbox_inches="tight") dpi is the resolution and bbox_inches="tight" trims the empty margin. Use .pdf instead of .png for something that stays sharp at any size, which is what you want in a thesis.
